 Eastern Washington looks to stop Utah Tech’s run game | Things to watch
 Nov. 13, 2026 
 Updated Fri., Nov. 13, 2026 at 10:32 p.m. 
 Add Spokesman-Review on Google
 By Dan Thompson 
 The Spokesman-Review
 Related
 Stories
 EWU, Idaho football both impacted by FAA ground stop 
 Malik Dotson has spent pretty much every day since July with the same group of football players, and he realizes that the end of that time is near.
 “I feel like we’re feeling joyful,” Dotson, a sixth-year running back for Eastern Washington, said Tuesday. “You’ve got to take in the rainy day. You’ve got to take in the cold for what it is, because this is the last two weeks with this group of people, and we put so much into it.”
 Through 10 games, the Eagles haven’t gotten as much out of this season as they would have liked. They are 2-8 overall and 1-6 in the Big Sky, and on Saturday they face the team they’re tied with at the bottom of the league standings: the Utah Tech Trailblazers (1-9, 1-6).
 Kickoff is set for 6 p.m. with the game streaming on ESPN+.
 “They probably should have won against Idaho State and UC Davis,” Eastern Washington head coach Aaron Best said of the Trailblazers’ most recent games, each of them seven-point losses. “They’re playing their best ball now, which doesn’t excite me a ton. We’ve got our work cut out for us.”
 As the Eagles look for their third win of the season, here are three aspects of the game to watch:
 1. Utah Tech’s running game. On a per-play basis, the Trailblazers have the second-worst offense in the league, averaging 5.0 yards per play.
 Eastern is hardly better by that metric – 5.1 yards per play – but the Eagles have executed 92 more plays than the Trailblazers have over the season, and that sheer difference in volume is essentially what has separated the two running games.
 Over their last two games, though, the Trailblazers have been particularly committed to running the football. They attempted a season-high 44 rushes two weeks ago against Idaho State and gained 164 yards, their second-most in a game this season. Last week they ran 40 times for 91 yards at UC Davis. Those correlate with their two closest losses of the season.
 “We’ve got to knuckle up,” EWU sophomore safety Seanje Finister said. “We know they’re going to come down and they’re going to run the ball and they’re going to do what they want to do. And we have to come ready.”
 Eastern Washington’s rushing defense has allowed 6.4 yards per carry, the most in the Big Sky.
 2. Eastern Washington’s passing game. Lately, the Eagles have been as healthy as they’ve been all season at wide receiver, strengthening a group they have leaned on to produce as Eastern’s running game has struggled.
 The Eagles have the fourth-most passing yards in the Big Sky (275.3) and are facing a Utah Tech passing defense that has allowed the second-fewest yards in the league this year (219.6 per game).
 “I think everybody in the receiver room is good from top to bottom,” said EWU sophomore Rylin Lang, who has 31 catches for 281 yards this season. “We have a lot of playmakers at receiver and I believe everyone is good enough to be in the game.”
 Redshirt junior quarterback Nate Bell’s favorite target has been redshirt senior Wesley Garrett, who leads the team with 46 catches for 588 yards. But redshirt sophomore Jaxon Branch, when healthy, has been the team’s best receiver. He has 20 catches for 284 yards and three touchdowns in just five games, two of which he left early because of injury.
 Bell has 2,656 passing yards this season and has a chance to be Eastern’s first 3,000-yard passer since Eric Barriere threw for 5,070 across 13 games in 2021.
 Bell was careful with the ball against Idaho, completing 17 of 24 throws with no interceptions. But he had just 174 yards and one touchdown with a long completion of 25 yards. That came after back-to-back three-interception games against Montana State and Montana.
 3. Eastern Washington’s playmakers on defense. The Eagles start four seniors on the defensive line and are talented at every level of the defense, most notably in the secondary. That’s where Bryce Smith, Jaylon Jenkins, Ambrose Marsh and JoJo Maxey-Johnson have developed a reputation as ballhawks: Between them they have nine interceptions and a fumble recovery.
 As bad as the Eagles have been at giving up big plays defensively, they have also produced plenty of turnovers and stops in key situations.
 So the question is: How well do they play, knowing that they still have eligibility left where many others on the defense do not?
 “This is football. We love football,” Finister said. “We’ve got a bunch of guys who come out here and are happy to be out here, and we’ve got a lot of guys who have two games left in their entire life. We (play) for them, for our brothers, our teammates, our coaches, our community.”
